speaker: Jigar Shah
title: Jigar Shah on the DOE's Role In Accelerating The Energy Transition
question: In clean energy, why do already-proven technologies with paying customers still struggle to attract private infrastructure investors?
guest: What happened on the technology front is America has figured out how to make things smaller and more bite-sized. It's the same solar panel that you put thousands of in one field to make utility-scale solar, or 12 of them on your roof for residential solar. When I first started SunEdison back in 2003, we had signed contracts with Whole Foods, Staples, IKEA, and others right away, and people said, 'That's great, but you only need $60 million of capital.' Most of these folks are like, 'Infrastructure investors don't get out of bed for less than $250 million.' If you can't aggregate up $250 million worth of projects, then you're not going to get any attention from us. So we ended up getting money from Goldman Sachs's special situations group, and they made a nice 17% rate of return to do the first set of deals. Once we got to that multi-hundred-million-dollar scale, we got Wells Fargo and Union Bank of California to come in. You have all these weird niche projects where you have very high rates of return for new technology, but it amounts to 25, 50, or 75 million initially of capital needed before it goes to trillion-dollar scale.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
This is the "missing middle" or commercialization "valley of death" problem: the technology works, but the project doesn't yet fit what infrastructure investors are built to buy.

Infrastructure funds price for low risk and low returns, so they want a track record of many operating plants at commercial scale, not one or two. A first-of-a-kind or early commercial plant still carries scale-up, construction-cost and performance risk, often without the fixed-price construction contracts, performance guarantees, warranties or insurance that lenders require. Having customers isn't enough either: offtake contracts are often too short, with counterparties that lack strong credit, or for products like green hydrogen or sustainable fuels that have no liquid market to fall back on, so revenues aren't considered bankable.

Meanwhile, the capital needed (tens to hundreds of millions) is too large for venture capital, and the returns too modest for it, while the risk is too high for infrastructure capital. Small deal sizes, expensive due diligence, policy uncertainty and high interest rates widen the gap. That is why public loan programs, green banks and blended or catalytic capital are often needed to fund the first few projects.

models.answer: Private infrastructure investors underwrite predictable, long-duration cash flows rather than technological proof or early commercial traction, creating a "missing middle" between venture capital and project finance. Even when a clean energy technology works and has paying customers, it often lacks institutional bankability: multi-year operating data at full commercial scale, creditworthy performance warranties, and fixed-price construction guarantees that cap cost-overrun and downtime risks. Early revenue also frequently comes from short-term contracts or unrated buyers rather than the decade-plus, investment-grade offtake agreements required to secure low-cost project debt. Meanwhile, early commercial deployments fall into a structural capital gap, proving too asset-heavy and low-margin for venture equity yet too small, bespoke, and unstandardized to justify the high due-diligence costs and large minimum check sizes of major infrastructure funds. Compounding these hurdles, external bottlenecks such as permitting delays, grid interconnection queues, immature supply chains, and policy uncertainty introduce schedule and cash-flow volatility that conservative, yield-focused infrastructure mandates are not built to absorb.

noweb.answer:
Proven clean energy technologies often fall into a "missing middle" between venture capital and traditional infrastructure finance. Infrastructure investors, such as pension funds, insurers, and project-finance banks, do not underwrite technology potential; they underwrite predictable, multi-decade cash flows with minimal downside risk. Even when a technology works and has paying customers, early commercial facilities rarely meet strict bankability standards. They typically lack multi-year operating histories at full scale, balance-sheet-backed performance warranties from creditworthy suppliers, and fixed-price construction guarantees that protect against cost overruns and delays.

Customer demand alone also does not equal bankable revenue if contracts are too short, exposed to commodity swings, or signed with buyers lacking investment-grade credit, which blocks the low-cost debt infrastructure returns depend on. Deal size compounds the mismatch: commercial plants are too capital-intensive and low-margin for venture equity, yet too small, bespoke, and illiquid to justify a major infrastructure fund's transaction costs. Until repeatable builds, insurance wraps, and long-term contracted offtake compress execution and revenue risks to bond-like levels, private infrastructure capital remains on the sidelines.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
This is usually called the "missing middle" or the second "valley of death," and it happens at the stage of moving from first commercial projects to replicable scale. The technology works and customers will pay, but the money needed falls between two kinds of investors.

Venture capital doesn't fit because these projects need hundreds of millions in hard assets and pay back slowly with modest returns, not the fast, outsized gains VC funds need. Infrastructure funds and lenders don't fit either, because they want low, predictable risk. They underwrite against long operating histories, proven costs to build and run, standard contracts and creditworthy long-term buyers. Early clean-energy plants often lack those things. Their offtake contracts may be short or with weak buyers. Supply chains, contractors and performance guarantees are often untested. Revenue can depend on changing policy or carbon prices. And many deals are too small or too unusual to justify the time and cost of due diligence.

"Proven" to an engineer is not the same as "bankable" to a financier. Closing the gap usually takes concessional or blended finance, government loan guarantees, insurance against underperformance, or standardized project structures that let deals be repeated.

models.answer: Private infrastructure investors are built to underwrite predictable, long-term cash flows rather than technology or execution risk, so technical proof and early customers are rarely enough to make a project "bankable." Even when a technology works, lenders and infrastructure funds look for multi-year commercial operating histories, turnkey construction contracts, and performance warranties backed by strong balance sheets—protections that young companies and early deployments seldom have. Similarly, having paying customers differs from having bankable revenue: investors typically require long-term, creditworthy offtake contracts, whereas early customers often sign shorter agreements, lack investment-grade credit, or leave projects exposed to volatile merchant energy prices. These projects also get caught in the "missing middle," where upfront capital needs are too large for venture capital yet individual deals are too small or bespoke to justify the high due-diligence costs of major infrastructure funds. Finally, permitting bottlenecks, grid interconnection delays, construction overruns, and shifting policy incentives can quickly erase the modest, bond-like returns that private infrastructure capital is designed to accept.

noweb.answer: Private infrastructure investors do not underwrite technical proof alone; they underwrite predictable, long-term cash flows that can support low-cost project debt. Even when a clean energy technology works and has paying customers, early commercial deployments often fall into a "missing middle" between venture capital and traditional infrastructure finance. Scaling from a pilot to commercial scale introduces construction, supply-chain, and integration risks, and without several years of operating data at scale, insurers and lenders cannot reliably model performance. Customers may also sign short-term, conditional, or non-investment-grade contracts rather than the long-term, bankable offtake agreements infrastructure funds require. Compounding this, project returns frequently depend on shifting tax credits, subsidies, or carbon policies, while lengthy permitting and grid-interconnection queues delay revenue. Because infrastructure capital is priced for low-risk, standardized assets, investors often wait until peers absorb the execution risks of the first few commercial plants before committing at scale.

A proven technology and paying customers show that the product works and people will buy it. Infrastructure investors need confidence that a specific project will generate enough predictable cash over many years to repay debt and earn a return.

Early projects often lack a long operating record, long-term contracts with creditworthy customers, or guarantees that cover construction delays and equipment failures. A customer may pay today but be unwilling to commit at a fixed price for ten years. Exposure to power prices, policy changes, or grid connection delays can further weaken the financial case. And when projects are small or each deal is structured differently, the cost of evaluating them can be too high relative to the investment.

That creates a financing gap. The technology is ready to deploy, but the first projects need patient or risk-tolerant capital to build the track record and repeatable contracts that mainstream infrastructure investors rely on.

That leaves investors exposed to construction delays, higher operating costs, or falling revenue. The result is a financing gap: the project needs more capital than venture investors typically provide, while its risks exceed what infrastructure investors can accept at their target returns.
